sentences.text: Reports described that effective tobacco control programs need to be comprehensive, with the goal of reducing tobacco use by preventing the initiation of tobacco use among young people, promoting quitting and eliminating non-smokers' exposure to environmental tobacco smoke.
A comprehensive approach to tobacco control includes school and community programs, public education, smoking cessation, legislation and enforcement, taxation and policy.
Studies found that multi-pronged approaches are required in order to reduce smoking, necessitating a broad coalition of partners working toward a common goal of smoking reduction and/or cessation.
Success in tobacco control will depend on comprehensive prevention and cessation programs, as well as on targeted tobacco control initiatives at both policy and legislative levels.
For countries that have adopted strong, comprehensive programs, smoking has leveled off or declined.

Evidence-based guidelines for successful youth tobacco programs include involving stakeholders, using interactive programs, connecting with broader tobacco reduction goals, using peer influence, building youth social and personal skills, using role models, encouraging family and community involvement, working across subject areas in school, keeping youth busy with other activities, providing nicotine replacement therapy where addiction is present, not accepting funding from tobacco companies, beginning programs early, and evaluating program effectiveness.

Alberta implemented four provincial youth tobacco programs in 2002: Teaming Up for Tobacco-Free Kids (Grades 4, 5 and 6, focused on prevention), Building Leadership for Action in Schools Today or BLAST (Grades 7, 8 and 9, focused on prevention, protection and cessation), Youth Action and Advisory Project or YAAP (Youth aged 14-17, focused on prevention, protection and cessation), and Kick the Nic (Youth aged 14-18, focused on cessation and protection).
Since 2000, the Kick the Nic program, a stop smoking program aimed at teens who want to quit smoking, continues to be implemented in schools and community organizations throughout the province.

Developing female-specific programs in prevention and cessation is necessary given the statistical trends and patterns of women's tobacco consumption, gender differences in the physiology and social psychology of smoking, women's particular experience of inequality, and strong woman-centred advertising and promotion by the tobacco companies.

Programs supported by Health and Welfare Canada in Saskatoon, Regina and Winnipeg, as well as programs in Quebec, Ontario, and Prince Edward Island, offered ideas for innovative programming for girls and women.

The Take Control program in Saskatoon was a 16-week group program for women, focussing on developing an holistic understanding of taking control of one's health and life, and some insight into smoking behaviour.

The Pregnant Women and Tobacco Smoking Cessation/Reduction Project in Regina was designed for young, pregnant, mostly native, teenage smokers, with the intervention design largely left to the young pregnant women and new mothers themselves.

Legislation that requires high prices for tobacco products deters use, particularly among youth, with research studies estimating that a 10% increase in tobacco prices results in an overall decrease in tobacco sales of 4% to 6%, with these decreases being even greater among youth.

Legislation restricting or prohibiting smoking in bars and restaurants does not negatively impact on sales or employment in the long term, with several studies finding that smoking restrictions actually increase sales.
An annual investment of $5 - $12 per person is required to implement tobacco control initiatives.
The cost of enforcing tobacco control legislation is highest in the first two years after laws have been introduced, after which costs tend to decline as the public becomes aware of new laws.

The Tobacco and Smoking Reduction Regulation in Alberta was developed and approved, prohibiting the furnishing of tobacco products to minors in public places, and banning smoking in vehicles with minors present.
Starting June 1, 2015, Alberta legislation mandated minimum pack sizes for specific tobacco products to eliminate smaller, less expensive options and banned flavoured tobacco products.

The Tobacco Reduction Youth Engagement Campaign in Alberta recruited seven schools and trained 365 students, of which 58 became actively engaged in the Campaign, with an independent evaluation showing that youth were successfully engaged through various activities including school, community, and publicity events, and youth-led projects.

Evaluation of Alberta's Tobacco Cessation Program at the Henwood Residential Treatment Centre with adults with addictions to alcohol and other drugs showed that this treatment group sustained smoking quit rates consistently higher than those typically found among Canadian smokers trying to quit smoking.

Health Canada's Tobacco Control program develops and implements initiatives to reduce or prevent the use of tobacco or the harm associated with continued tobacco use by various methods such as prevention and cessation education, regulation and compliance, research, evaluation and surveillance, and mass media campaigns.
